state.context: Can I32 fixes HTTP handlers as callable http::server_response (http::request) emits []. Every Can function must carry mandatory assertions, and a probe compiling a handler fails with no eligible declaration for the request argument because no Can expression produces http::request: requests enter only through runtime ingress snapshots, and P10 defines no request constructor. P12 nevertheless requires supplied-completion callback assertions for every handler behavior row. P3 states that opaque fixture handles compare by compiler-issued harness-token identity, and existing when-rows name in-scope opaque locals such as encoded bytes. Reader calls inside a handler body can therefore carry when-rows naming req, but the root assertion call still needs a request-typed argument expression. Staged integration can enter compiled handlers through a private test bridge with real snapshots. The catalogue is closed and test-only execution paths are disfavored.

assertions.instructions: Which design best reconciles mandatory handler assertions with ingress-only requests?

criteria.elided_scope: Assertion rows omit ingress-only opaque root arguments; the checker verifies the omission covers exactly those positions, the runner supplies harness-token requests, and body reader calls must carry when-rows with supplied outcomes.
criteria.token_constructor: Add one closed assertion-only catalogue constructor returning http::request; the checker rejects it outside assertion contexts, the runner supplies a harness token, and body reader calls must carry when-rows with supplied outcomes.
criteria.real_harness_request: Add one closed assertion-only catalogue constructor with descriptive inputs; the runner builds real request snapshots through the shared snapshotRequest adapter so body readers execute for real without when-rows.
criteria.staged_only: Exempt mounted handlers from mandatory Can assertions by explicit design correction; handler bodies are still type-checked, and staged loopback integration through the test bridge supplies all execution evidence.
